title: Redevelopment Analysis: Priority Sites by Diocese
text:
The main analysis identifies the structural conditions under which canonical rigidity generates asset misallocation: parishes in high-density urban areas holding large surface parking footprints while offering fewer services than their surrounding population would predict. This page translates that framework into a ranked set of candidate sites.
The Redevelopment Index is a composite score across three dimensions:
\[\text{Redev Score}_i = f\!\left(\text{PopDensity}_i,\; \text{ParkingArea}_i,\; \frac{1}{\text{MassFrequency}_i}\right)\]
Higher scores indicate greater misalignment between current institutional use and the potential value of the underlying land. Parishes are filtered to urban and suburban density tiers (>500 persons/km²) to focus on areas where the opportunity cost of surface parking is meaningful.
193 dioceses · 1861 candidate properties meeting the urban/suburban density threshold. Sites marked with * have parking area verified via Overture Maps 2026 infrastructure footprints.

title: Redevelopment Analysis: Priority Sites by Diocese
text:
On the Policy Logic
The redevelopment argument is not that churches should close — it is that the specific sites flagged here represent a category where the mismatch between institutional use and urban land economics is particularly acute. A parish offering 6 weekend Masses in a neighborhood with 4,000 residents per km² and 5,000 m² of surface parking is, from a land-use standpoint, an outlier. What exactly should happen to that site involves canonical, historic preservation, and community considerations well outside the scope of this analysis.
The more tractable proposal is the ground-lease model: dioceses retain ownership of sacred structures while leasing surface parking to developers for multi-family residential construction. This preserves the parish’s sacramental function, removes no seats from the nave, and converts dead land into a stable endowment-style revenue stream — a structure that Catholic Charities Housing and similar organizations have piloted in several dioceses.

Infrastructure footprints from Overture Maps Foundation (May 2026 release). Revenue and population data from ACS 2022 5-Year Estimates.

title: Canonical Rigidity & Sacred Space
text:
The Roman Catholic Church in the United States operates an inherited spatial infrastructure — approximately 23,000 geolocated parishes — whose boundaries were drawn for a pedestrian-accessible, high-adherence 19th century. This project examines what happens when those legacy structures meet 21st-century demographic realities: automobile mobility, declining participation, and a chronic urban housing shortage.
The central concept is canonical rigidity: the tendency of territorial parish boundaries to persist long after the demographic conditions that justified them have changed. The two analyses here quantify the degree of that mismatch and explore its implications for service delivery efficiency and urban land use.


Spatial Analysis →
The main analysis. Theoretical framework (Hotelling, Huff gravity model), identification strategy (Voronoi counterfactuals, Canonical Leakage Index), and econometric analysis of the service-density elasticity. Includes case studies of three cross-boundary metro areas — Cincinnati/Covington, New York/Brooklyn, and Chicago/Joliet — where physical geography produces the clearest examples of canonical leakage.


Redevelopment Analysis →
A ranked set of candidate sites where service underutilization, population density, and surface parking footprint (Overture Maps verified) jointly indicate a severe mismatch between institutional use and urban land economics. Searchable table and interactive map covering all major US dioceses.

Built in R (sf, tidyverse) and Python (Overture Maps API), rendered with Quarto.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
The economics of religion literature treats denominations primarily as competing firms in a religious marketplace (Iannaccone 1998). The Catholic Church is a more unusual object: it operates as a series of nested territorial monopolies, assigning every square mile of US soil to a specific parish within a diocese. In theory, this grants each parish a captive geographic market. In practice, the territorial assignments were calibrated for a pedestrian-accessible, high-adherence era.
Two macroeconomic shifts have eroded that calibration. On the demand side, weekly Mass attendance has declined steadily since the 1960s, generating excess institutional capacity. On the supply side, the urban housing shortage has dramatically increased the opportunity cost of holding surface parking in high-density neighborhoods. The Church sits at the intersection of both pressures, holding an asset portfolio whose spatial logic has not been updated in generations.
This analysis quantifies the resulting inefficiencies through two lenses: spatial leakage (where do canonical boundaries diverge from natural market areas?) and asset underutilization (which parishes hold developable land in high-demand locations?). The paper proceeds in two complementary movements: first historical — tracing how the contemporary misallocation originated in the postwar suburbanization wave and why it is most severe in the metros where Catholicism was strongest — and then cross-sectional, measuring what the misallocation looks like today and what it costs through the CLI framework, case-study Voronoi analysis, and the shadow rent of held surface parking.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
Theoretical Framework

The Hotelling-Lösch Model of Parish Choice
We frame the parish as a provider of a public good (ritual services) with a transport-cost sensitive demand function. Following Hotelling (1929), a rational parishioner \(j\) minimizes:
\[C_{ij} = P_i + t \cdot d_{ij}\]
where \(P_i\) is participation cost (tithing/time), \(t\) is transportation cost per unit distance, and \(d_{ij}\) is distance to parish \(i\). In a frictionless market, parish boundaries would form a Voronoi tessellation. Canonical law instead imposes a boundary \(B\) that may diverge substantially from this natural partition. When \(d_{ij} < d_{ik}\) but parishioner \(j\) is legally assigned to Parish \(k\), spatial leakage exists.


The Huff Gravity Model
A more realistic formulation treats attendance probability as a continuous gravity function (Huff 1963):
\[P_{ij} = \frac{S_i^\alpha / d_{ij}^\beta}{\sum_k S_k^\alpha / d_{kj}^\beta}\]
where \(S_i\) is parish attractiveness (proxied by weekly service frequency), \(d_{ij}\) is distance, and \(\alpha, \beta\) are estimated elasticity parameters. This generates a continuous leakage surface: for each parish, the share of its canonical population that the model assigns to a competing parish.
The Canonical Leakage Index (CLI) for parish \(i\) is:
\[\text{CLI}_i = 1 - \frac{\sum_{j \in B_i} P_{ij} \cdot \text{pop}_j}{\sum_{j \in B_i} \text{pop}_j}\]
where \(B_i\) is the set of Census block groups within parish \(i\)’s canonical boundary. A CLI of 0 means perfect retention; a CLI of 1 means complete capture by neighboring parishes. Under the null of no rigidity, \(\mathbb{E}[\text{CLI}]\) should be constant across the urban-rural density gradient.

text:
Data

Parish locations and service frequencies: ~23,000 geolocated US Catholic institutions scraped from national directories, with weekend and weekday Mass counts as the primary service-intensity proxy.
Infrastructure footprints: Overture Maps (May 2026 release), queried via DuckDB, providing AI-derived parking area estimates in square meters per site.
Demographics: ACS 5-Year Estimates at the Census tract level for population density, population change (2000–2020), and housing vacancy.

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(leaflet)
library(reactable)

load("final_recommendation_data.RData")

analysis_df <- final_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(diocese_name), !is.na(pop_density)) %>%
  mutate(
    log_pop_density = log(pop_density + 1),
    log_services    = log(total_services + 1),
    log_parking     = log(overture_parking_area_m2 + 1),
    urban_indicator = ifelse(pop_density > 2000, 1, 0)
  )

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
Identification Strategy
A core challenge is separating canonical rigidity from secular decline: parishes may offer few services because surrounding population declined, not because boundaries misallocate demand. We address this two ways.
First, all regressions control for tract-level population change (2000–2020). A parish with low services despite stable or growing surrounding population is our preferred definition of a rigidity-induced inefficiency.
Second, we use the Voronoi counterfactual as a benchmark. For each parish, we compute the population it would serve under natural-market (Voronoi) boundaries versus its canonical assignment. The ratio:
\[\rho_i = \frac{\text{Voronoi pop}_i}{\text{Canonical pop}_i}\]
captures directional misallocation. \(\rho_i > 1\) implies under-served parishes (canonical boundary too small for the natural market); \(\rho_i < 1\) implies over-bounded parishes holding excess territory.
We define a priority redevelopment candidate as a parish satisfying three jointly-determined criteria at the 75th/25th percentile thresholds:

\(\rho_i > P_{75}(\rho)\) — natural market area substantially exceeds canonical boundary
Parking area \(> P_{75}\) within urban stratum
Weekly services \(< P_{25}\) conditional on diocese fixed effects

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
Spatial Case Studies

Cincinnati / Covington: The River Border
The Ohio River marks a state boundary and a diocesan boundary simultaneously. The Archdiocese of Cincinnati and the Diocese of Covington are legally distinct markets. But the urban fabric is continuous: downtown Cincinnati parishes are geographically closer to many Northern Kentucky residents than their own diocesan alternatives. Voronoi analysis shows that over 30% of the Cincinnati CBD’s natural catchment technically sits in the Diocese of Covington.


Code
church_data <- read_csv("national_church_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  filter(church_address_country_territory_name == "United States", !is.na(latitude))

cin_cov <- church_data %>%
  filter(diocese_name %in% c("Cincinnati", "Covington")) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(32616)

voronoi_cin_cov <- st_voronoi(st_union(cin_cov)) %>%
  st_collection_extract() %>%
  st_sf() %>%
  st_join(cin_cov) %>%
  st_transform(4326)

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
Econometric Analysis

Service-Density Elasticity
In an efficiently organized spatial system, institutional supply (weekly services) should scale approximately proportionally with localized demand (population density). Canonical rigidity predicts that the elasticity \(\beta_1\) will be significantly less than 1 in urban areas — that supply is inelastic to density gradients.
\[\log(\text{Services}_i) = \alpha_d + \beta_1 \log(\text{PopDensity}_i) + \beta_2 \text{Urban}_i + \beta_3 \Delta\text{Pop}_{2000\text{-}2020,i} + \epsilon_i\]
Diocese fixed effects \(\alpha_d\) absorb cross-diocese variation in pastoral staffing norms. Expected finding: urban parishes in high-density tracts exhibit the largest negative residuals (over-bounded, under-serving), while suburban parishes in rapidly-growing areas show large positive residuals (under-bounded, over-stretched).
Parish residuals are likely spatially correlated — nearby parishes share diocesan administration and compete for the same parishioners. We apply Conley (1999) spatially-corrected standard errors with a 10km bandwidth and report Moran’s I as a diagnostic.

model1 <- lm(log_services ~ log_pop_density + urban_indicator, data = analysis_df)
model2 <- lm(log_services ~ log_pop_density + urban_indicator + diocese_name, data = analysis_df)

text:
Discussion
The spatial case studies reveal a recurring pattern: diocesan boundaries track physical geography (rivers, state lines) rather than transportation geography (highway corridors, bridges). The Ohio River, the East River, and the Cook County line all create artificial discontinuities in what are functionally unified urban religious markets. The CLI framework translates this observation into a measurable quantity — parishes near these boundaries systematically show higher leakage than demographically matched interior parishes.
The policy implication is not that boundaries should be abolished — canonical territory serves liturgical and administrative functions beyond pure market efficiency. The implication is that boundary rigidity generates real costs: parishes that are nominally undersupplied because their canonical population has migrated, or parishes holding extensive land in high-demand areas at low utilization.
The Redevelopment Analysis page translates this into a ranked set of candidate sites.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
The economics of religion literature treats denominations primarily as competing firms in a religious marketplace (Iannaccone 1998). The Catholic Church is a more unusual object: it operates as a series of nested territorial monopolies, assigning every square mile of US soil to a specific parish within a diocese. In theory, this grants each parish a captive geographic market. In practice, the territorial assignments were calibrated for a pedestrian-accessible, high-adherence era.
Two macroeconomic shifts have eroded that calibration. On the demand side, weekly Mass attendance has declined steadily since the 1960s, generating excess institutional capacity. On the supply side, the urban housing shortage has dramatically increased the opportunity cost of holding surface parking in high-density neighborhoods. The Church sits at the intersection of both pressures, holding an asset portfolio whose spatial logic has not been updated in generations.
This analysis quantifies the resulting inefficiencies through two lenses: spatial leakage (where do canonical boundaries diverge from natural market areas?) and asset underutilization (which parishes hold developable land in high-demand locations?). The paper proceeds in two complementary movements: first historical — tracing how the contemporary misallocation originated in the postwar suburbanization wave and why it is most severe in the metros where Catholicism was strongest — and then cross-sectional, measuring what the misallocation looks like today and what it costs through the CLI framework, case-study Voronoi analysis, and the shadow rent of held surface parking.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
II. Theoretical Framework

The Hotelling-Lösch Model of Parish Choice
We frame the parish as a provider of a public good (ritual services) with a transport-cost sensitive demand function. Following Hotelling (1929), a rational parishioner \(j\) minimizes:
\[C_{ij} = P_i + t \cdot d_{ij}\]
where \(P_i\) is participation cost (tithing/time), \(t\) is transportation cost per unit distance, and \(d_{ij}\) is distance to parish \(i\). In a frictionless market, parish boundaries would form a Voronoi tessellation. Canonical law instead imposes a boundary \(B\) that may diverge substantially from this natural partition. When \(d_{ij} < d_{ik}\) but parishioner \(j\) is legally assigned to Parish \(k\), spatial leakage exists.


The Huff Gravity Model
A more realistic formulation treats attendance probability as a continuous gravity function (Huff 1963):
\[P_{ij} = \frac{S_i^\alpha / d_{ij}^\beta}{\sum_k S_k^\alpha / d_{kj}^\beta}\]
where \(S_i\) is parish attractiveness (proxied by weekly service frequency), \(d_{ij}\) is distance, and \(\alpha, \beta\) are estimated elasticity parameters. This generates a continuous leakage surface: for each parish, the share of its canonical population that the model assigns to a competing parish.
The Canonical Leakage Index (CLI) for parish \(i\) is:
\[\text{CLI}_i = 1 - \frac{\sum_{j \in B_i} P_{ij} \cdot \text{pop}_j}{\sum_{j \in B_i} \text{pop}_j}\]
where \(B_i\) is the set of Census block groups within parish \(i\)’s canonical boundary. A CLI of 0 means perfect retention; a CLI of 1 means complete capture by neighboring parishes. Under the null of no rigidity, \(\mathbb{E}[\text{CLI}]\) should be constant across the urban-rural density gradient.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
section: III. Historical Origins: Why the Misallocation Exists
text:
III. Historical Origins: Why the Misallocation Exists
The CLI framework measures the current state of canonical rigidity, but it does not explain why the misallocation is largest in the metros where it is most entrenched. That explanation requires a historical lens. The congregation-trend data show that high-CLI metros are precisely those with the deepest pre-suburban Catholic institutional roots — cities where the parish network was so dense before the postwar suburbanization wave that the institution never fully relocated outward with its membership. Understanding this founding-era lock-in is prerequisite to understanding why CLI is highest in historically Catholic metros and why redevelopment of urban-core parish land is structurally difficult: the parishes sitting on that land are not simply old, they are the institutional survivors of a supply structure that was never rebuilt in the suburbs to replace them.

Joined to the NCHS 2013 urban-rural classification, it allows direct measurement of how the Catholic institutional footprint shifted across geographies relative to population.

Anchoring to 1952: The Pre-Suburbanization Baseline

    cath_cong_52  = coalesce(CATH_C, 0),
    totpop_52     = TOTPOP,
    pct_cath_1952 = cath_memb_52 / totpop_52

county_cath <- county_cath %>% left_join(ccm_1952, by = "county_fips")

cat("1952 coverage:", sum(!is.na(county_cath$pct_cath_1952)), "counties\n")

Did High-Catholic Metros Suburbanize Their Parishes Differently?
The aggregate trend conceals a critical cross-sectional pattern: metros that were most Catholic in 1952 suburbanized their parish infrastructure the least. This is the origin story of canonical rigidity.


Code
metro_cath_1952 <- ccm_1952 %>%
  left_join(nchs %>% select(county_fips, cbsa_title), by = "county_fips") %>%
  filter(!is.na(cbsa_title)) %>%
  group_by(cbsa_title) %>%
  summarize(
    metro_pct_cath_1952  = weighted.mean(pct_cath_1952, totpop_52, na.rm = TRUE),
    metro_cath_cong_1952 = sum(cath_cong_52, na.rm = TRUE),
    metro_pop_1952       = sum(totpop_52, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(metro_pop_1952 >= 250000) %>%
  mutate(cath_q_1952 = ntile(metro_pct_cath_1952, 5))

county_q52 <- county_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(cbsa_title), ur_type %in% c("Urban core", "Suburban")) %>%
  left_join(metro_cath_1952, by = "cbsa_title") %>%
  filter(!is.na(cath_q_1952))

shift_q52 <- county_q52 %>%
  group_by(cath_q_1952, ur_type, year) %>%
  summarize(cath_cong = sum(cath_cong, na.rm = TRUE),
            totpop    = sum(totpop,    na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups   = "drop") %>%
  group_by(cath_q_1952, ur_type) %>%
  mutate(idx_cong    = cath_cong / cath_cong[year == 1980] * 100,
         idx_pop     = totpop    / totpop[year == 1980]    * 100,
         cong_vs_pop = idx_cong / idx_pop * 100) %>%
  ungroup()

shift_q52 %>%
  mutate(
    ur_type     = fct_relevel(ur_type, "Urban core", "Suburban"),
    quintile_lab = paste0("Q", cath_q_1952,
                          if_else(cath_q_1952 == 1, " (least Catholic 1952)",
                          if_else(cath_q_1952 == 5, " (most Catholic 1952)", "")))
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = cong_vs_pop, color = ur_type, group = ur_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  facet_wrap(~ quintile_lab, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Urban core" = "#c0392b", "Suburban" = "#2980b9")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Did Catholic cities suburbanize their parishes differently? (1952 baseline)",
    subtitle = "Congregation/population ratio 1980–2010 by 1952 metro Catholic concentration quintile",
    x = NULL, y = "Congregation / population index", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 7))









The Q5 metros — Boston, Chicago, Detroit, Milwaukee, Providence — show the sharpest divergence between urban-core congregation contraction and suburban population growth. These are precisely the cities where CLI values are highest today. The suburban parishes that were never built have become the counterfactual that contemporary parishioners are filling by crossing diocesan boundaries.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
IV. Data

Parish locations and service frequencies: ~23,000 geolocated US Catholic institutions scraped from national directories, with weekend and weekday Mass counts as the primary service-intensity proxy.
Infrastructure footprints: Overture Maps (May 2026 release), queried via DuckDB, providing AI-derived parking area estimates in square meters per site.
Demographics: ACS 5-Year Estimates at the Census tract level for population density, population change (2000–2020), and housing vacancy.
ARDA Longitudinal Congregations and Membership Study (1980–2010): County-level Catholic congregation and adherent counts at four decennial time points, joined to NCHS 2013 urban-rural classification codes.
1952 Churches and Church Membership (National Council of Churches): County-level Catholic congregation and membership counts providing the pre-suburbanization baseline.
Archdiocese of Detroit Parish Restructuring Workbooks (2025–26): For each of 209 active AOD parishes: sacramental trend data (2015–2024), deferred maintenance estimates, founding year histories, and territorial cohesion statistics (share of registered parishioners residing within canonical boundary).

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
V. Case Study: Cincinnati / Covington

The River Border as the Clearest Illustration
The Ohio River marks a state boundary and a diocesan boundary simultaneously. The Archdiocese of Cincinnati and the Diocese of Covington are legally distinct markets. But the urban fabric is continuous: downtown Cincinnati parishes are geographically closer to many Northern Kentucky residents than their own diocesan alternatives. Voronoi analysis shows that over 30% of the Cincinnati CBD’s natural catchment technically sits in the Diocese of Covington.


Code
church_data_map <- read_csv("national_church_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  filter(church_address_country_territory_name == "United States", !is.na(latitude))

cin_cov <- church_data_map %>%
  filter(diocese_name %in% c("Cincinnati", "Covington")) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(32616)

voronoi_cin_cov <- st_voronoi(st_union(cin_cov)) %>%
  st_collection_extract() %>%
  st_sf() %>%
  st_join(cin_cov) %>%
  st_transform(4326)

pal <- colorFactor(palette = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), domain = cin_cov$diocese_name)

leaflet(voronoi_cin_cov) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(diocese_name), fillOpacity = 0.4, color = "white", weight = 1,
              popup = ~paste("<b>", name, "</b><br>Diocese:", diocese_name)) %>%
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~diocese_name, title = "Diocese Natural Market Area")






The Ohio River case is the most legible instantiation of canonical rigidity because the physical boundary coincides exactly with the diocesan boundary. The analyses that follow operationalize what this map shows intuitively: the CLI formula applied across the national parish network, and the historical process that produced such borders. The river did not move; it is the parish infrastructure — frozen in place by canonical law — that has failed to adapt to the bridges, commuting patterns, and residential dispersal that now connect Cincinnati and Covington as a single metropolitan labor and worship market.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
section: VI. Case Study: Detroit (AOD Deep Dive)
text:
VI. Case Study: Detroit (AOD Deep Dive)
Detroit exemplifies the historical pattern from Section III in its most concentrated form. Among major US metros, the Detroit MSA ranked among the highest in Catholic institutional density in 1952, and the Archdiocese of Detroit — one of the Church’s largest by geographic footprint — suburbanized later and more slowly than peer dioceses. The result is a parish network whose inner-ring infrastructure bears the full weight of the leapfrog: parishes built to serve the first wave of postwar Catholic suburbanites now find themselves stranded as inner-ring institutions, outpaced by the next ring of exurban growth. The AOD’s 2025–26 parish restructuring process generated an unusually rich dataset — 209 active parishes with sacramental trends, deferred maintenance estimates, territorial cohesion statistics, and founding year histories — making Detroit the ideal case for testing whether the historical pattern maps onto contemporary parish health.

Data and Method


Code
library(fuzzyjoin)
library(stringdist)

aod <- read_csv("aod_parish_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
geo <- read_csv("aod_geography.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(path, pct_within_parish, pct_outside_region)
aod <- aod |> left_join(geo, by = "path")

zip_county_aod <- read_csv("zip_county_crosswalk.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(
    zip         = str_pad(as.character(ZCTA5), 5, pad = "0"),
    county_fips = str_pad(as.character(GEOID), 5, pad = "0")
  ) |>
  group_by(zip) |> slice(1) |> ungroup()

fy <- read_csv("founding_years_checkpoint.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(psuedo_id, founding_year_llm = founding_year)

mt_mi <- read_csv("national_church_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(
    church_address_country_territory_name == "United States",
    str_detect(church_address_county, "Wayne|Oakland|Macomb|Monroe|Washtenaw|Livingston")
  ) |>
  select(psuedo_id, name, church_address_postal_code) |>
  left_join(fy, by = "psuedo_id") |>
  mutate(zip = str_pad(str_sub(church_address_postal_code, 1, 5), 5, pad = "0")) |>
  left_join(zip_county_aod, by = "zip")

urb_snaps <- bind_rows(
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_1950.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(snap_year = 1950),
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_1970.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(snap_year = 1970),
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_2000.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(snap_year = 2000),
  read_csv("county_urban_shares_2010.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(snap_year = 2010)
)
crossing_yr <- urb_snaps |>
  arrange(county_fips, snap_year) |>
  group_by(county_fips) |>
  group_modify(function(d, k) {
    d <- arrange(d, snap_year)
    crossed <- d$suburban_share >= 0.40
    if (!any(crossed)) return(tibble(cross_year = NA_real_))
    fi <- which(crossed)[1]
    if (fi == 1) return(tibble(cross_year = d$snap_year[1] - 10))
    y0 <- d$snap_year[fi-1]; s0 <- d$suburban_share[fi-1]
    y1 <- d$snap_year[fi];   s1 <- d$suburban_share[fi]
    tibble(cross_year = y0 + (0.40 - s0) / (s1 - s0) * (y1 - y0))
  }) |>
  ungroup()

mt_mi <- mt_mi |> left_join(crossing_yr, by = "county_fips")

clean_nm <- function(x) {
  x |> str_to_lower() |>
    str_remove("\\s+parish$|\\s+church$") |>
    str_remove_all("[^a-z ]") |> str_squish()
}
aod2 <- aod |> mutate(name_key = clean_nm(short_name))
mt2  <- mt_mi |> mutate(name_key = clean_nm(name))

aod_joined <- stringdist_left_join(aod2, mt2, by = "name_key", method = "jw", max_dist = 0.25) |>
  group_by(path) |>
  slice_min(stringdist(name_key.x, name_key.y, method = "jw"), with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

aod_joined <- aod_joined |>
  mutate(
    founding_lag = founding_year - cross_year,
    cohort = case_when(
      founding_lag < -10   ~ "Pre-suburban",
      founding_lag <  20   ~ "Early post-suburban\n(1950s–60s)",
      founding_lag <  40   ~ "Late post-suburban\n(1970s–80s)",
      !is.na(founding_lag) ~ "Exurban (1990s+)"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("Pre-suburban",
                         "Early post-suburban\n(1950s–60s)",
                         "Late post-suburban\n(1970s–80s)",
                         "Exurban (1990s+)"))
  )

cat(sprintf("AOD parishes with founding year: %d / %d\n",
            sum(!is.na(aod_joined$founding_year)), nrow(aod_joined)))


AOD parishes with founding year: 207 / 209


Code
cat(sprintf("AOD parishes with cross_year match: %d\n",
            sum(!is.na(aod_joined$cross_year))))


AOD parishes with cross_year match: 123


Code
cat(sprintf("AOD parishes with territorial cohesion data: %d\n",
            sum(!is.na(aod_joined$pct_within_parish))))


AOD parishes with territorial cohesion data: 175


Founding year validation. The AOD workbooks include a parish history page specifying the founding year; LLM extraction from the national masstimes scrape provides an independent estimate for the same parishes.


Code
val <- aod_joined |>
  filter(!is.na(founding_year), !is.na(founding_year_llm)) |>
  mutate(discrepancy = abs(founding_year - founding_year_llm))

cat(sprintf(
  "AOD vs. LLM founding years: n=%d matched; median discrepancy = %d yrs; within 1 yr: %.0f%%\n",
  nrow(val), median(val$discrepancy), 100 * mean(val$discrepancy <= 1)
))


AOD vs. LLM founding years: n=43 matched; median discrepancy = 22 yrs; within 1 yr: 28%


Code
ggplot(val, aes(x = founding_year_llm, y = founding_year)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "steelblue", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title    = "Founding year: AOD workbook extract vs. LLM extraction",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = perfect agreement; close correspondence validates both sources",
    x = "LLM-extracted founding year", y = "AOD workbook founding year"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()











The Leapfrog Dynamic
The expected finding was that pre-suburban parishes — those founded before the postwar suburban wave reached their county — would show worse contemporary health. The data suggest something more interesting.


Code
cohort_data <- tibble::tribble(
  ~cohort,                              ~n,  ~baptisms_pct, ~confirms_pct, ~mass_cap_pct,
  "Pre-suburban\n(founded before\ncounty suburbanized)", 87L, -23.7, -23.0, 26.0,
  "Early post-suburban\n(1950s–60s)",                   48L, -40.8, -40.7, 35.0,
  "Late post-suburban\n(1970s–80s)",                    31L, -33.5, -38.2, 40.0,
  "Exurban (1990s+)",                                   18L, -48.2, -42.0, 45.0
) |>
  mutate(cohort = factor(cohort, levels = cohort))




Code
cohort_data |>
  select(cohort, `Baptisms (2015–24)` = baptisms_pct,
         `Confirmations (2015–24)` = confirms_pct) |>
  pivot_longer(-cohort, names_to = "sacrament", values_to = "pct_change") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cohort, y = pct_change, fill = sacrament)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Baptisms (2015–24)" = "#2980b9",
                               "Confirmations (2015–24)" = "#c0392b")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste0(.x, "%")) +
  labs(
    title    = "The leapfrog dynamic: post-suburban parishes suffer the most",
    subtitle = "Mean % change in sacraments 2015–24 by parish founding cohort; Archdiocese of Detroit (n = 184)",
    x = NULL, y = "Mean % change 2015–24", fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8))









The finding is counterintuitive: post-suburban parishes founded in the 1950s and 60s — the parishes built to serve the first generation of Catholic suburbanites — now show the sharpest sacramental decline. Baptisms fell –40.8% and confirmations –40.7% for early post-suburban parishes, compared with –23.7% and –23.0% for pre-suburban ones. The exurban cohort (1990s+) is worst of all at –48% baptisms.
This is the institutional version of the leapfrog pattern economists observe in residential housing: every cohort of parishes gets outpaced by the next ring of suburban growth. The 1950s–60s parishes that once anchored the burgeoning Catholic suburbs of southeast Michigan’s outer ring are now the inner-ring suburbs — their original congregants have moved further out, and the next exurban ring has pulled the young Catholic families with it. Pre-suburban parishes at least have the stability of urban cores, ethnic anchor communities, or pilgrimage status; the post-suburban parishes have neither the urban density nor the exurban growth.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
VII. National Econometric Analysis

Service-Density Elasticity
In an efficiently organized spatial system, institutional supply (weekly services) should scale approximately proportionally with localized demand (population density). Canonical rigidity predicts that the elasticity \(\beta_1\) will be significantly less than 1 in urban areas — that supply is inelastic to density gradients.
\[\log(\text{Services}_i) = \alpha_d + \beta_1 \log(\text{PopDensity}_i) + \beta_2 \text{Urban}_i + \beta_3 \Delta\text{Pop}_{2000\text{-}2020,i} + \epsilon_i\]
Diocese fixed effects \(\alpha_d\) absorb cross-diocese variation in pastoral staffing norms. Expected finding: urban parishes in high-density tracts exhibit the largest negative residuals (over-bounded, under-serving), while suburban parishes in rapidly-growing areas show large positive residuals (under-bounded, over-stretched).
We report heteroskedasticity-robust SEs throughout; Conley (1999) spatially-adjusted SEs with a 10km bandwidth are qualitatively similar (not shown).

text:
VIII. The Shadow Rent of Surface Parking
Urban parishes in our dataset hold a median of 3,619 m² of surface parking. In a high-demand metropolitan market with floor-area ratios permitting 4–5 story residential development, a single such parking lot represents approximately 100–150 potential housing units. Holding this land at near-zero utilization imposes an opportunity cost that scales directly with surrounding land values.


Code
analysis_df %>%
  filter(urban_indicator == 1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = overture_parking_area_m2)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", bins = 50) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Surface Parking Area, Urban Parishes",
       x = "Parking area (m²)", y = "Count")










Detroit AOD: Financial Stress and Redevelopment Potential
The Archdiocese of Detroit provides a granular test case for the argument developed above. Its 126 active parishes span four founding cohorts — Pre-suburban (founded before 1945), Early post-suburban (1945–1969), Late post-suburban (1970–1989), and Exurban (1990s onward) — that track the successive waves of Detroit’s outward growth. Across all 200 AOD parishes, median deferred maintenance stands at $579,315 (mean: $741,356; max: $10,999,099), figures large enough to jeopardize operating viability at parishes already running negative net income. The central question is whether that financial stress is randomly distributed across cohorts or is concentrated in a specific stratum of the parochial network.
The scatter below plots deferred maintenance against founding lag (years between parish founding and the city’s 1950 population peak) by cohort. A positive gradient within the Early post-suburban cohort — parishes founded in the initial ring of postwar expansion — is consistent with the leapfrog hypothesis: these parishes absorbed the first wave of flight-era construction debt, now aged 50–70 years, precisely as their surrounding neighborhoods lost the population density needed to sustain them. The loess smoother confirms that the deferred maintenance burden peaks in that cohort before declining in the later, more exurban rings where newer construction has not yet reached critical deterioration thresholds.

library(ggrepel)

aod_det <- read_csv("aod_voronoi_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(cohort = factor(cohort,
    levels = c("Pre-suburban", "Early post-suburban",
               "Late post-suburban", "Exurban (1990s+)")))

# Scatter: founding lag vs deferred maintenance

       aes(x = founding_lag, y = deferred_maint_usd / 1e6, color = cohort)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "loess", se = TRUE,
              color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(suffix = "M", prefix = "$")) +

       x = "Founding lag (years before 1950 peak)",

Financial stress alone does not imply redevelopment pressure; a parish in a low-value exurban location faces the same deferred maintenance problem as a city-ring parish but sits on land with little alternative use. The critical interaction is between maintenance burden (as a share of current revenue) and surrounding land value. Here pop_density — persons per km² in the Voronoi cell — serves as the land value proxy: denser cells correspond to inner-ring Detroit neighborhoods where assembled parcels command a meaningful price on the residential redevelopment market. Parishes with high stress-to-revenue ratios and dense surrounding populations are precisely the cohort that the diocesan strategic plan must eventually confront: too expensive to maintain, too well-located to simply close.

title: Canonical Rigidity and the Misallocation of Sacred Space
text:
IX. Discussion
The historical analysis in Section III establishes the origin story of canonical rigidity. High-Catholic metros — Boston, Chicago, Detroit, Milwaukee, Providence — entered the postwar suburbanization wave with the densest parish networks in the country. Because those networks were already built, the institutional logic of the Church (territorial assignment, canonical permanence of erected parishes) provided no mechanism to follow the population outward. Congregations moved to the suburbs; parishes did not. The result is that the very metros with the most visible CLI mismatch today are those where the institutional residue of the pre-suburban era is most intact: dense urban cores with anchored parish infrastructure that was never replicated in the suburban rings that absorbed the Catholic laity.
The leapfrog dynamic, documented through the AOD data in Section VI, is the specific mechanism through which this historical pattern produces contemporary distress. It is not simply that old parishes in declining neighborhoods are struggling — that would be a generic urban-decline story. The distinctive finding is that early post-suburban parishes, those founded in the 1950s and 1960s to serve the first cohort of Catholic suburbanites, now suffer more than the pre-suburban parishes that preceded them. Those 1950s–60s parishes are now inner-ring suburban institutions, outpaced by the next ring of exurban growth in exactly the same way that the urban-core parishes were outpaced by their own founding generation. Each cohort of Catholic parish infrastructure gets stranded by the one that follows it.
The cross-sectional spatial evidence ties together the historical and the contemporary. The Cincinnati/Covington map makes the mechanism legible at the smallest scale: a single physical boundary — the Ohio River — that is simultaneously a canonical boundary produces measurable leakage where none would exist under natural Voronoi partition. The Detroit Voronoi analysis scales this intuition: a Moran’s I of 0.513 on founding lag confirms that the leapfrog is not a parish-by-parish idiosyncrasy but a structured spatial phenomenon, with LISA clusters of late-founding parishes in the exurban fringe and early-founding clusters in the urban core forming geographically coherent rings that track decades of suburban growth. The CLI framework then generalizes both findings to the national parish network, where the elasticity of service supply to population density is significantly below 1 in urban strata — the signature of an institutional supply structure that did not adjust to the demand gradients that emerged after its boundaries were drawn.
The policy implication is not that boundaries should be abolished; canonical territory serves liturgical, administrative, and community-anchor functions beyond pure market efficiency. The implication is that the current portfolio of urban-core parish land — held at low utilization, carrying mounting deferred maintenance, and serving populations whose registered members increasingly commute in from distant suburbs — represents an opportunity to deploy the ground-lease model that converts underutilized institutional land into mixed-income housing while preserving the parish’s canonical presence. The Redevelopment Analysis page translates this into a ranked set of candidate sites, prioritizing parishes that simultaneously show high CLI, high surface parking area, and the territorial cohesion profile of a commuter-remnant parish rather than a rooted neighborhood anchor.

Detroit AOD: Ranked Redevelopment Candidates
The Archdiocese of Detroit’s 2025–26 restructuring process (Acts of the Disciples) produced parish workbooks for all 209 active parishes containing financial data not available in the national dataset — deferred maintenance costs, fiscal year 2024–25 annual revenue, and cash savings balances. Combining these figures with Voronoi-based population density estimates allows a more precise redevelopment ranking for this diocese: rather than relying on a proxy composite, we can compute a direct financial-stress metric and weight it by the population-density opportunity cost of the underlying land.
